item.title: Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).

In 2027, Australian author Helen Garner will be feted with the Hadada, a prize that recognizes a writer’s lifelong literary contributions. I am here as an independent body to hype this choice.

Garner—a novelist, journalist, and diarist—writes big-hearted heroines who are often on the edge of a crisis. Her other fans include Lauren Groff, Lily King, Rumaan Alam, and Ben Lerner, but we are legion. Why, you ask?

In a recent piece for The Guardian, Emma Brockes also praised Garner’s “ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth.” And it’s true—that earthiness is what makes her work indelible. But it’s also just the tip of an iceberg.

Here are three of Garner’s best known books (and why you should make like the Parisians and pick them up, stat).

Monkey Grip, Garner’s 1977 debut, sent a shockwave through Australia. This novel chronicles a woman’s doomed-from-the-jump situationship with a heroin addict who charms her intermittently as they orbit a communal living situation.

A little like Susie Boyt’s sleeper hit, Loved and Missed, this book beautifully captures the recurring heartbreak involved in loving an addict. But it’s never saccharine, or sanctimonious.

Following a bohemian Melbourne milieu that echoes the author’s own set at the time, Garner’s non-judgmental portrait of freewheeling radicals brought out the moralizers on publication. Nora, our heroine, ruffled feathers for depicting ambivalent parenthood administered with a very loose latchkey. All adults in this book are libidinally motivated. Drugs and sex are world-structuring forces.

But what’s most exciting is how naked the prose is about all of that want. In Garner’s matter-of-fact voice, Nora’s thirst for the grifting Javo is rendered tender, abject, holy, and pathetic by turns. She feels like a real and vulnerable person with a mighty human flaw. The best kind of protagonist.

My favorite of Garner’s novels is The Children’s Bach. Another tale of domestic upheaval ignited by a charismatic chaos agent, this book traces the happily partnered Athena Fox’s infatuation with a blast from the past. Against reason, she leaves her partner and two small children for… a rock star.

What follows is a little predictable, but as with Monkey Grip the pleasure is in experiencing that slow road to ruin. (Or is it ecstasy?)

The third person POV serves this book, which manages to texturize everyone affected by Athena’s choices. She feels like a modern Nora, in the Ibsen sense.

The Spare Room is a cool, slim, spiky book. I find this Garner still gnaws at me. Following two semi-estranged old friends who fall back together when one seeks harbor following a terminal diagnosis, this novel depicts the unpleasant side of caretaking and the indignity of illness.

This book asks some truly itchy questions. Such as, what do you do when your patient is delusional—and/or, you want them out of your house?

As in the other novels, our protagonist chafes against conventionality and obligatory mutual obligation. And her extreme honesty hits you like a glass of cold water. As always, there’s a nakedness to a Garner subject. She doesn’t flinch from depicting those ugly emotions or unwanted thoughts.

In a review for the Times, Daphne Merkin once compared Garner to other “laconic and wayward,” ladies who specialize in the “art of artlessness, like Jean Rhys, Jane Bowles and Paula Fox.”

I agree with wayward, but I think that artful eye is in a class all its own. Do yourself a favor and join the Helen hive. Today.

item.title: Filmmaker Ava DuVernay challenges the stories America tells about itself in '14th'
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Filmmaker Ava DuVernay challenges the stories America tells about itself in '14th'

A decade after examining the 13th Amendment and its connection to mass incarceration, DuVernay has a new documentary about the 14th Amendment and the struggle over citizenship and equal rights.

TONYA MOSLEY, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. Who gets to belong in America? It's a question the country confronted after the Civil War when some 4 million enslaved people gained their freedom. In 1868, the 14th Amendment established birthright citizenship and guaranteed due process and equal protection under the law. But those promises were contested almost from the beginning.

In her new documentary, "14th," my guest today, filmmaker Ava DuVernay, traces the struggle over these rights from the extraordinary possibilities of Reconstruction and the backlash that followed to the present-day battles over citizenship, equality and presidential power.

DuVernay has built a body of work that challenges the stories America tells about itself, often connecting personal experiences to larger questions of race, history and power. Her films include "Selma," about the Civil Rights Movement, "Origin," an exploration of caste, and the Oscar-nominated documentary "13th" about race and mass incarceration. She also created the acclaimed television dramas "When They See Us" about the wrongful convictions of the Central Park Five and "Queen Sugar" about a Black family in Louisiana. DuVernay began making "14th" during Donald Trump's campaign for a second term and has said making the documentary became a way to channel her own fear and anger about the direction of this country.

Ava DuVernay, welcome back to Fresh Air.

AVA DUVERNAY: Thank you. It's always so wonderful to sit with you, although somewhat intimidating because you have the best voice on radio. So my kind of scratchy voice here is no comparison, but I'll do my best to keep up.

MOSLEY: Oh, I appreciate it...

DUVERNAY: (Laughter).

MOSLEY: ...So much. Thank you for the compliment.

DUVERNAY: It's true.

MOSLEY: But, you know, starting - I mean, knowing that you started this to channel your fear and anxiety, I'm just wondering how you're feeling now post-midterms.

DUVERNAY: Gosh. Well, it's pretty recent. And I feel good about the information and ideas that we're sharing in "14th." I'm hopeful that by people watching the film and interacting with the film, challenging the film, thinking about the film and what's in it, that there'll be some guidance from history on how to move forward. But without some kind of grounding and common language, a common vocabulary and understanding as to where we are now, I fear that this moment will slip away.

And I feel like we're in a time of celebration. But, you know, the vote should just be the beginning. And a big part of what we talk about in "14th" is the fact that we've been trained not to do anything much in between the votes as citizens. And this is really what we all need to look at and step up to right now.

MOSLEY: One of your subjects calls the 14th Amendment the workhorse of the Constitution. Can you say more about that? Why? What would Americans lose without it?

DUVERNAY: Well, I love this part of the documentary because we have a montage of all of our different experts - over 50 historians, scholars, politicians, even a contractor, librarians, podcasters - talking about the 14th Amendment and how to describe it in one line. Stacey Abrams calls it the everything bagel. And it is so much of what we hold dear as Americans.

First, I am an American because I was born here or because I am naturalized, right? That's just a base-level understanding. The next is, I am equal to the person next to me because I am American. These are just basic tenets. These are the things that we believe as Americans, that we abide by, right? The next is, I am protected by my citizenship, right? If I am arrested, am I - if I am accused of something, there is a process that is due to me - is a way to think about that, right? That we have certain rights in our voting mechanisms, that we can depend on Congress to advocate for us.

These are just some key facts of our citizenship that most people consider to be a given. But it's not a given because it's at risk. And not only is it at risk. It's under direct attack. And that's what the film steps through piece by piece, to show how this has really been a sinister strategy that's been unfolding on many levels - political, economic, social, cultural. And it's raging at a even higher level and a more expedited velocity than it ever has been.

MOSLEY: Experts in the film call the 14th Amendment a constitutional reset after the Civil War because they needed something that makes sure that equality was embedded into the law of the land. Can you lay out exactly what that means?

DUVERNAY: Yes. I mean, the Constitution before the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendment didn't have the word equal in it as it related to human beings.

MOSLEY: Right.

DUVERNAY: Before the Reconstruction Amendments, as they're known, Black people were considered three-fifths of a human being.

MOSLEY: Yeah.

DUVERNAY: And the catalyst for the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendment were the rights of African American people after the Civil War. These 4 million people had to be dealt with. So 13th said they are no longer property.

MOSLEY: Yeah.

DUVERNAY: OK? They are full human beings. They're not three-fifths of a human being anymore. 14th Amendment said, OK. Oh. Saying that they're free weren't - wasn't enough. They are citizens. OK, everybody? OK. We're going to come back on the 15th. They can vote. OK? Let's just keep getting more and more clear. So this was all around the impetus for the rights that so many people enjoy, right? The rights that have been gained because of the 14th Amendment for women, for Asian Americans, for, you know, people with disabilities, for children.…

Here’s the shortlist for the first-ever Children’s Booker Prize.

Today, the Booker Prize Foundation announced the “Great Eight” shortlist of titles for inaugural Children’s Booker Prize, which will be awarded annually beginning in 2027. The Children’s Booker is the latest off-shoot of the prestigious Booker Prize (most recently awarded to M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything) and celebrates fiction for eight- to 12-year-olds, written in or translated into English and published in the UK or Ireland. The winner will take home £50,000 and the Booker Foundation will be donating at least 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books to children across the United Kingdom and Ireland.

“Any of these books stands comparison with any adult book, whatever the category, on its own terms,” said Frank Cottrell-Boyce, Chair of the Children’s Booker Prize 2027 judges, in the shortlist announcement. He, along with fellow judges Sanchita Basu De Sarkar and Lolly Adefope, narrowed down the shortlist from 89 submissions and will be joined for the final decision by four young people: Ibrahim (12), Lainey (12), Luna (8), and Myla (11).

Here’s the shortlist:

Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts, The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen

Catherine Bruton, Tadpole Summer

Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano, War

Iqbal Hussain, The Night I Borrowed Time

Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, The Teller of Tall Tales

Mikey Please, The Rambler’s Curse

Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor, Séamus Almost Famous

Shaun Tan, Hometown

The winner will be announced in a ceremony on February 2, 2027.

Drew Broussard

Drew Broussard is the bookstores editor-at-large for Literary Hub and the host of The Lit Hub Podcast. His writing has appeared around the internet and in friends' mailboxes. After a decade working at The Public Theater, he decamped to the woods of upstate New York, where he now lives. He is the manager of Rough Draft Bar & Books in Kingston, NY.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

In 'GTA VI,' every stolen car is a music discovery machine

Each time a 'Grand Theft Auto VI' player enters a new vehicle, the in-game radio opens a rabbit hole for curious listeners

If you've ever wondered what it might feel like to lead cops on a high-speed chase through downtown Miami as Young Thug croons, "Hustlers don't stop, they keep going," Grand Theft Auto VI has you covered. The massive open-world action game, which turns a one-to-one recreation of Florida's central hotspot — dubbed Vice City, Leonida — into the playpen for a Bonnie and Clyde-style outlaw campaign, is largely powered by music. There are currently more than 800 songs in the game, all of which have been spun off into bespoke radio stations representing the vibrant music culture of the place it simulates. Early into my playthrough, Kevin Lyttle's 2003 soca hit "Turn Me On" blared out of a speedboat's onboard radio as I pulled up to a yacht party, creating a unique thrill as the familiar suddenly became new again.

The most anticipated video game sequel of all time, and now among the most successful entertainment properties ever, GTA VI follows military vet Jason Duval and new parolee Lucia Caminos as they repair their broken relationship, cutting their teeth in a high-stakes criminal megalopolis with hopes of regaining custody of their son. Players split time between the two characters, playing linear missions that advance the story, triggering side quests that spiral into all corners of a vast map, or testing the limits of the open world by doing, well, whatever they want. Where similar games allow the user to "fast travel," or teleport, to important areas, GTA values the scenic route, the atmosphere that linear travel creates. And since hijacking rides is a core mechanic, that atmosphere is always changing: Each time you pull the door shut on a new exotic whip, helicopter or airboat, that vehicle's radio kicks on one of more than 20 stations spanning pop, rock, hip-hop, jazz, dance and classical. As reggaeton artist Rauw Alejandro noted of his playing experience in an interview with Billboard, "Sometimes, I wasn't even doing the missions — I was just vibing, discovering new things, listening to the music on the radio."

The need to spend lots of time driving around in cars makes the user a captive audience, and as such, the radio is a pipeline — to old songs, newer songs, new-to-you songs and even a few new-to-everyone songs. A previously unreleased D'Angelo track can be found on the Gilles Peterson-hosted station Worldwide FM. When Jason picks Lucia up from prison, "Crazy for You," a new song by Lana Del Rey, plays as they start their desperado journey together. Premieres from Burna Boy, Kali Uchis & Helado Negro, Zara Larsson and Cardi B are scattered across the stations. Beyond the exclusives, one of which pairs SZA with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, are relatively recent songs given new life by the narrative. Two versions of Carly Rae Jepsen's cult classic "Run Away with Me" soundtrack key scenes in the early game, a jet ski excursion turned supercar race to the nightclub NINE1NINE — and when Jason and Lucia get there, Tove Lo and SG Lewis' dance sleeper "Heat" is blaring. Deeper in are songs that will be familiar to many but are transformed by context. The couple's first string of robberies together has a sync so perfect I dare not spoil it.

The gameplay of GTA VI opens the door to a unique kind of sonic immersion, one that straddles classic radio functionality and the unique surreality that only video game storytelling allows. On one hand, the radio experience exposes players to a distinctly old-world curation on a scale that maybe isn't possible anywhere else, given the size of the player base. On the other, it treats most in-game playback like needle drops in a movie: highly subjective, there to make the player feel as much as possible like the star.

There are just enough songs that each playthrough will be slightly different for every player, but the sensations are comparable. When I went to dump a car that belonged to Jason's co-worker Donnie, a volatile, coke-addled drug mule fed to pigs by rival swamp gang the Kingfishers, the V-Rock station was blasting "Nothin' but a Good Time" by Poison, which felt like high irony. Donnie was a screw-up whose incompetence led directly to his demise, and as I sank his red '85 Blista in the marsh, the song's cries in pursuit of a more exciting life rang out like an unlikely funeral dirge. Echoing the game's broader attention to detail, the radio serves as an entry point into the inner lives of the characters who populate its world, and a window into its broader attempt to render a dynamic culture.

Of course, at least some of the charm is that these are, overtly, not real radio stations, and that the surrounding culture is a trick mirror. The hosts are often celebrities of distinct pedigree playing off their public perceptions — "Weird Al" Yankovic and Brigitte Nielsen, Robyn and model Alex Consani, Buddy Guy and Keith Richards, Bad Bunny and RaiNao. The ads that pop up between songs are absurd and satirical. In a talk-radio segment, the Brazilian singer Anitta plays "Dr. Nita," a quack giving sex advice. The hold the radio exerts on you as a player is tied up in the game's blown-out otherworldliness.…

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Eighty-one-year-old Bob Windrem spent half his life at NBC News. As a senior investigative producer, he drew on CIA sources to feed Tom Brokaw early info on the September 11 terrorist attacks. He filed stories about the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and cartel violence in Mexico, and went undercover in Johannesburg to help reveal Israel’s role in South Africa’s missile development program. Today, he’s perhaps best known as “Net Income,” the name under which he’s chronicled the Brooklyn Nets for more than two decades. James Herbert’s profile is an entertaining look at the journalistic chops of an octogenarian NBA blogger who kept his hard-news edge, and the most interesting guy lurking just outside the locker room.

Before he’d written a word for NetsDaily, Windrem was the main character on the NJ.com forum. Many posters hated how he defended the front office’s decision to let Kenyon Martin walk in 2004. The personal attacks he receives now can be a bit much, but Windrem either throws a jab back or rolls his eyes. “I’m a big boy. I’ve been yelled at by members of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and the White House press secretary and TV anchors,” he said. He can handle a few mean tweets.

A few basketball stories where the drama is off the court

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

PEN Writes US Emerges as Free Speech Group “For Writers, by Writers”

Big names in literature are attached to an aspiring PEN Center that launched this week. Omar El Akkad, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Carmen Maria Machado, Sarah McNally, and Percival Everett are among the heavyweights listed as founding members of PEN Writes Us. More than 100 writers, artists, translators, and more are attached to the free speech group.

Pulitzer Prize-winning author and founding member M. Gessen said in a press release announcing the launch:

“I have watched, in more than one country, how the space for speech closes: not all at once, but one exception at a time – one category of speech declared too dangerous, one publisher persuaded to stay quiet. A PEN center’s job is to refuse the exceptions. The United States needs a center that will defend protected speech without carve-outs for whatever is politically inconvenient this year.”

A former PEN America president is among the founding members. Author Dinaw Mengestu resigned as president after the organization released a report about cultural boycotts and the “rising isolation and exclusion” of Israeli and Jewish writers.

PEN Writes US is “dedicated to defending free expression, supporting writers and artists at risk, and championing reading, translation and literature.” The group will seek to join more than 140 PEN centers at the PEN International Congress in September 2027.

Voting Begins for the Final Round of the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards

The opening round of the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards started November 10th and ended November 22nd. Now, the final round of voting has begun, and it runs until November 29th. The winners are announced December 3rd.

There are books in 15 categories to vote for: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Mystery & Thriller, Romance, Romantasy, Fantasy, Science Fiction, Horror, Debut Novel, Audiobook, Young Adult Fantasy & Sci-Fi, Young Adult Fiction, Nonfiction, Memoir, and History & Biography. These categories are unchanged from last year.

The Goodreads Choice Awards offer the most blatant popularity contest of all the year-end awards: you don’t need to have read all the books in a category to vote for the “best” one. In fact, you don’t even need to have read the book you’re voting for. That introduces a host of problems, and that’s before getting into the fact that Amazon owns Goodreads. Still, it makes for a good snapshot of the books getting the most attention at this point in time.

You can vote on the Goodreads website.

The New York Times Shares Their 100 Notable Books of 2026

The New York Times list falls somewhere in the middle, with 100 fiction and nonfiction books selected by NYT staff.

As you might expect, there are a lot of literary fiction books represented, like American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee, The Disappearers by Marlon James, and Canon by Paige Lewis. But plenty of other genres make an appearance, including romance (Star Shipped by Cat Sebastian), horror (Off the Reservation by Stephen Graham Jones), science fiction (Earth 7 by Deb Olin Unferth), and cultural history (Darkology by Rhae Lynn Barnes).

You’ll find familiar titles here, like the bestselling Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke and Strangers by Belle Burden, as well as the Booker Prize-winning The End of Everything by M. John Harris. There are also books that have been on many of the other best books of the year lists, like John of John by Douglas Stuart.

Mixed in are some more obscure picks, including Korean Messiah by Jonathan Cheng, The Radiance by Ayad Akhtar, and It Will Come Back to You by Sigrid Nunez.

You can find the full list at The New York Times. They also offer a cheat sheet for selecting your first read off the list.
